Priority campaign: Control your own narrative

Why now (internal): Internal context: Airbnb announced (about 20–21 Oct) that for bookings from 20 November 2026 hosts can't require bigger checkout tasks (stripping beds, washing and putting away dishes, laundry, taking rubbish outside). Small requests stay (plates in the sink, used towels gathered, sorting rubbish into indoor bins). Host fines are banned, and rules show more prominently on listings. Information isn't restricted: hosts can still tell guests anything about their home. Content only hints at the change (a light nod at most, never an explanation of the rule) and never names the platform, uses its logo or its coral colour, or misstates the rule.

The angle: hosts can no longer require much of guests at checkout, and they’re frustrated. We barely hint at that change, never name the platform, take the hosts’ side and give them back what they control: their own narrative. Humanise the host, share what guests need to know (bin day, how the home works), and respectful guests look after it as a self-catering home, not a hotel. DigiStayBook is where that story and information live.

28 items, 2026-10-29 to 2026-11-25, on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Reddit, Facebook groups, YouTube Shorts, Pinterest, the blog, LinkedIn and email. Week 1 is written in full and its Facebook card, carousel and Reel are made (marked Written Made); weeks 2–4 are in outline. Set each item’s status here; it saves with the rest of your review.

The message

Your welcome, in your words.

Every home has a story. Tell yours. Control your own narrative.

Why this angle: hosts are frustrated and feel they’ve lost control of their own homes. We take their side, barely hint at the cause and hand them back something they do control: their voice. The platform limited what hosts can require; it didn’t limit what they can say. Guests who know the host, and know how the home works, treat it like a home rather than a hotel.

Four content pillars

  1. Narrative (hosts): every home has a story; take back the welcome.
  2. Humanise: the person behind the listing: their name, why they bought the place, the story behind the furniture.
  3. Information: bin day, which bin is which, how the heating works. Information, never demands; always allowed.
  4. Respect and memories (guests): a home you’re borrowing, not a hotel; past guests’ memories set the tone. (Plus light Community and Product items.)
Always
  • Hint, don’t explain: lead with homes, hosts and stories. At most a light nod (“a lot of hosts have felt their say has been taken away”). Never spell out the rule or list what can’t be asked.
  • Lean on the words: control your own narrative, your home your story, humanise, respect, home not hotel, your welcome in your words, everything guests need to know.
  • Write house info as information (“bin day is Tuesday”), not instruction (“take the bins out”).
  • Host-facing: empowering, not bitter. Guest-facing: warm, never guilt-tripping.
  • Use real hosts’ stories only with permission; label the demo property as a demo.
Never
  • Name Airbnb, use its logo, its coral colour or look-alike wordplay.
  • Misstate the rule. It limits what hosts can require, not what they can say; never claim information is banned.
  • Suggest DigiStayBook is a way to make guests do chores, or promise guests will clean.
  • Promote the boycott or tell hosts to leave a platform.
  • Promise less damage, fewer complaints, better reviews or more bookings; invent stories; use fake accounts or vote manipulation on Reddit.

Who we’re talking to

  • Hosts with one or a few holiday homes who care about their place and want guests to feel it. They are the customers.
  • Guests and travellers (TikTok, Instagram): the respect message builds goodwill and makes hosts want to share it.
  • Property managers (LinkedIn, Reddit): later conversations, not this month’s focus.

Needs you

Before any of this goes out

  1. Review the 28 outlines below: confirm, ask for changes or skip each one.
  2. Start date is Thu 29 Oct to catch the news while it’s hot. This overlaps the current Facebook month (23 Oct – 21 Nov) on Facebook. See “Overlap” above.
  3. Create or confirm accounts: Instagram, TikTok (business account), a named founder account on Reddit, Pinterest business.
  4. Find one or two willing hosts (or use your own property) for the changeover, story and guestbook videos.
  5. Decide the call to action: follow only, or link to the website demo. That depends on launch status.
  6. Email items need an opted-in list and an email tool first.

Sat 31 Oct · Reddit · Discussion post

What's one thing in your welcome note that changed how guests treated your place?

Pillar: Community · Week 1: Control your own narrative
The post
Not made yet.Text post on purpose: host subreddits reward a real question, and a stock photo would read as an ad.
Written with it
Post title 
What's one thing in your welcome note that changed how guests treated your place?
Post text 
I keep hearing that the small, specific lines do the most, like "Every summer someone forgets their thongs under the deck. They're in the box by the door."

Hosts with one or two places especially: what's the line or habit that actually made a difference for you?

There's a lot of talk about checkout at the moment and I'm not here to add to it. I'm more interested in the part that's always been in our control.

Things I've seen hosts try:

- A welcome note that says who you are, not just the Wi-Fi password
- Meeting guests on arrival, or a short video hello
- Telling the story of the home (who painted the front door yellow, why there's an old fishing rod over the door)
- Writing house info as information, e.g. "collection is Monday, yellow lid is recycling" rather than "take the bins out"
- A guestbook, paper or digital, where past guests leave notes

Does any of it change how places are left? What would you add, and what's been a waste of time?

Disclosure: I'm building a digital welcome book for hosts, so I'm genuinely trying to learn what hosts value. I'm not linking it here, but happy to answer if anyone asks.
Reply templates
Reply · Someone shares what works 
That's a great one, thanks. Did you notice a difference straight away, or more over a season?
Reply · Someone is angry about the policy 
Completely understand. It's your place and you want it looked after. Out of interest, is there anything you've found that still helps, even a little?
Reply · Someone asks what you're building 
It's called DigiStayBook. A QR code in the house opens the host's welcome, the house info and a guestbook wall. I built it, so I'm biased; happy to hear what you'd want in one.
Hook

A specific question hosts can answer from experience, from a clearly named founder account.

Visual

Text post on purpose: host subreddits reward a real question, and a stock photo would read as an ad.

Call to action

No link; quote only with permission.

⚠ Naming the platform is fine in a Reddit discussion if hosts do; our own posts and comments still don't.

Mon 2 Nov · Facebook groups · Helpful reply

Be the calm voice in host threads

Pillar: Community · Week 1: Control your own narrative
The post

Edit in Canva ↗

Written with it
Reply · A frustrated "what do we do now?" thread 
Totally get it. It's your place and you want it looked after. One thing that helps, whatever the platforms allow: tell guests who you are and how the house works. "Collection is Wednesday, yellow lid is recycling" isn't a rule, it's information, and most people are happy to help once they know whose home it is.
Reply · "What should I put in my welcome?" 
I'd keep it to five things: who you are (a name and a line about why you love the place), a bit of the home's story, how the tricky things work (hot water, the sticky door), bin day and which bin is which, and your favourite local spots. Write it like you'd tell a friend staying over, not like a list of rules.
Reply · Someone asks for tools or apps (only where the group allows it) 
Full disclosure, I built one, so I'm biased: DigiStayBook puts your welcome, the house info and a guestbook behind a QR code. Happy to answer questions, and plenty of hosts do just fine with a well-written printed folder too.
Hook

Host groups are full of frustrated threads. Offer the constructive angle.

Visual

A shareable checklist image, '5 things worth telling every guest', on a real photo of a sunlit table. Posted with the reply where the group allows images.

Call to action

None. Help and listen.

The aim is to learn which short-term rental hosts recognise the problem, earn useful conversations and make the product easy to understand before launch. Keep the current Facebook-first approach. No new prices, launch promises or sign-up links in this month's copy.

Status, caption edits and comments save in this browser. They do not change Meta or write back to the NAS file. Use Copy my review or Download review to hand over the changes. Mark Drafted, Scheduled or Posted only after the corresponding action is verified in Meta.

Strategy & audience

The job of the month

Primary audience: Australian short-term rental hosts and owner-managers with one or a few holiday properties, especially those already answering guest questions or leaving a paper guide or guestbook. This is the working audience, to test through conversations—not a validated market-size claim.

Positioning: one QR display opens your welcome, house guidance, local favourites and a guest memory wall. Guests use their phone's browser without creating an account. The product is for a stay; it is not a tool for collecting booking-platform ratings.

Four messages to test

  1. Arrival: let guests find the next useful answer.
  2. Local knowledge: make the welcome feel personal.
  3. Memories: invite a note or photo without a guest sign-up.
  4. Host control: explain preview, approval and moderation accurately.

Boundaries for the copy

  • Prelaunch CTA: follow the Page or answer one useful question. Launch availability is announced only when ready.
  • Use genuine product screens and the real logo. Label the made-up demo property and sample messages. No invented customers, testimonials or poll results.
  • No promises of fewer messages, more bookings, better ratings, higher income or perfect automated screening.
  • No paid ads in this month. Proposed cash budget: A$0, using existing assets. Reserve roughly 3–4 hours a week for production, review and responding, then adjust to actual effort.
  • Keep private credentials, real guest data and private in-stay links out of public artwork.
  • Narrative campaign (from 29 Oct): hint at the platform change lightly, never spell it out, and never name Airbnb, use its logo or colour, or misstate the rule (it limits what hosts can require, not what they can say). Never suggest guests must clean.

Campaign, weekly rhythm & production

A better welcome, one scan away

Dates: 23 October–21 November 2026. Four full weeks plus two closing days. There is no discount, promo code or artificial deadline.

WeekFocusLearning question
1Make the arrival easierWhich arrival questions do hosts recognise?
2Put local knowledge to workWhat local tips feel useful?
3Give the property a memoryWhich memory prompt gets a response?
4Show the host's sideWhat prevents a host trying the product?
5Listen, then choose the next monthWhat should the next walkthrough answer?

One weekly production block

  1. Read genuine host replies and the last scorecard. Keep names and private messages out of artwork.
  2. Prepare the week's two feed graphics, carousel slides, reel and Story cards from the briefs. Use existing real demo captures or record current product screens.
  3. Review captions, demo labels, legibility, alt text and every visible product claim.
  4. After the owner's review, create native drafts where supported. Schedule only the approved final assets and confirm their times in Meta.
  5. Spend a short daily block responding to comments. Keep a weekly record of the questions, not invented quotes.

Five reels have shot-by-shot scripts; four carousels have slide outlines. A reference image or script is not an exported video or finished carousel. New content starts at Planned for that reason.

Needs you · decisions and checks

Before anything new goes out

  1. Priority campaign: review its 28 items (week 1 written and partly made), set up Instagram, TikTok and a named founder Reddit account, and decide the Facebook overlap (see the campaign).
  2. Review the 30 captions and visual briefs here. Approve, request changes or skip each item.
  3. Check the existing 19–22 October items in Business Suite before adding new drafts. Their recorded statuses below were imported from the earlier plan, not reverified today.
  4. Confirm the public website destination before changing the follow-only CTA to a demo or sign-up link. The current plan intentionally makes no public-domain or launch-date promise.
  5. Complete the launch checks and resolve the recorded testing issues before announcing general availability. The NAS testing checklist is the place to record proof.
  6. Decide on Instagram separately if you want it. This month works as a Facebook-only plan.
Weekly scorecard & next-month decision

What would make the month useful?

Working learning targets, not forecasts: collect at least ten substantive host replies and hold five willing-host conversations across the month. Establish the actual starting follower and reach numbers before interpreting growth. Do not report zero where a metric is unavailable.

MeasureRecordDecision it supports
FollowersStart/end from Page InsightsIs the intended audience starting to gather?
Reach and engagementPer post and format; record denominatorsWhich topics merit another attempt?
Substantive host repliesCount actual hosting questions or experience, not emoji-only repliesDoes the problem resonate?
Reel watch dataAvailable watch/completion measures in MetaDo people reach the explanation?
Production effortMinutes spent by formatCan the cadence be maintained?
Willing-host conversationsCount and anonymised themes; quote only with permissionWhat still needs explaining or changing?

Review dates

29 October, 5 November, 12 November and 19 November; final review 21 November. Compare formats cautiously if their reach is small or different. Keep the strongest useful topic, rewrite the weak explanation and choose the next month's cadence from evidence. No paid-ad spend is triggered automatically.

Conversation prompts: How do guests find your house information now? What do they ask again? Where does the current approach work well? What would stop you using a digital guestbook? What would you need to see in a demo?
